title: GOD NEVER ASKED YOU TO BE THANKFUL FOR WHAT BROKE YOU
paragraphs: GOD NEVER ASKED YOU TO BE THANKFUL FOR WHAT BROKE YOU
“Give Thanks in All Circumstances” — The One Word Paul Used That Changes Everything About Suffering, Gratitude, and the God Who Refuses to Abandon You
There is a Bible verse that has been quoted to people while they were barely holding themselves together.
Sometimes it was spoken with love.
Sometimes it was spoken by someone who had no idea how deeply the person standing in front of them was hurting.
And sometimes, instead of bringing comfort, it made an already wounded Christian feel guilty for bleeding.
“Give thanks in all circumstances.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:18
You have heard it before.
Maybe someone quoted it when your marriage was falling apart.
When the doctor gave you news you were not prepared to hear.
When you buried someone you thought you would grow old with.
When the person who promised never to leave became the very reason you struggled to trust anyone again.
Or when you were sitting alone, staring at bills you could not pay, wondering how a faithful God could allow His child to feel so abandoned.
And somewhere between the tears and the exhaustion, you began asking yourself a question you were almost ashamed to admit.
How am I supposed to thank God for this?
But what if the question itself came from a misunderstanding of the verse?
What if God was never commanding you to call your tragedy beautiful?
What if Paul was not telling you to celebrate the betrayal, praise the disease, or pretend the funeral did not shatter your heart?
What if the very Scripture that has made you feel guilty for grieving was actually written to teach you how to remain close to Jesus while you grieve?
Because there is something in the original Greek that deserves our attention.
Something small.
Something easily overlooked.
Something that may change how you understand gratitude for the rest of your life.
Paul did not say, “Give thanks for everything.”
He said something far more profound.
And to understand why that matters, we need to go back to what he actually wrote.
In 1 Thessalonians 5:18, the Greek text reads:
ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε· τοῦτο γὰρ θέλημα θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς.
Transliteration:
En panti eucharisteite; touto gar thelēma theou en Christō Iēsou eis hymas.
A close translation is:
“In everything give thanks; for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus.”
Notice those first two Greek words.
ἐν παντί — en panti.
In every circumstance.
In every situation.
In all things.
The preposition ἐν (en) ordinarily carries the sense of “in,” “within,” or “among,” depending on context.
Here, joined with παντί (panti), it expresses the comprehensive circumstances in which believers are called to give thanks.
That distinction matters.
Paul is commanding thanksgiving in every circumstance. He is not explicitly commanding us to regard every event itself as good.
This is not permission to become ungrateful when life is painful.
It is an invitation to discover that gratitude can exist even when life is painful.
And the rest of the verse makes the foundation unmistakable.
“For this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus.”
Not merely positive thinking.
Not pretending your circumstances are harmless.
Not convincing yourself that suffering is pleasant.
In Christ Jesus.
That is where Christian thanksgiving begins.
And that is where its deepest meaning is found.
Because there is an enormous difference between thanking God for the evil someone committed against you and thanking God that the evil someone committed against you cannot separate you from His love.
There is a difference between celebrating a diagnosis and thanking Jesus that sickness does not have the final authority over your eternal future.
There is a difference between calling death good and thanking Christ that He has conquered death.
There is a difference between pretending your heart is not broken and bringing every broken piece to the Savior who was wounded for sinners.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something that should have been said a long time ago.
You do not have to lie about your pain to be faithful to God.
You do not have to smile at the grave.
You do not have to call abuse a blessing.
You do not have to thank God for another person's cruelty as though cruelty were holy.
You do not have to pretend your disappointment is joy.
You can weep.
You can tremble.
You can admit you are exhausted.
You can say, “Lord, I do not understand.”
And you can still belong completely to Jesus Christ.
Because the Bible does not portray faith as the absence of tears.
It portrays faith as learning where to bring them.
Think about Jesus standing outside the tomb of Lazarus.
He knew what He was about to do.
He knew Lazarus would rise.
He knew death was about to surrender its temporary grip.
And yet John 11:35 records two of the most astonishing words in Scripture.
“Jesus wept.”
The Son of God did not stand outside that tomb rebuking everyone for grieving.
He did not accuse Mary and Martha of spiritual weakness because their hearts were broken.
He entered their sorrow.
He saw their tears.
And He wept.
Do you understand what that means?
The One who knew resurrection was coming still considered grief worthy of tears.
So why do we sometimes demand that wounded Christians act more emotionally detached than Jesus Himself?
Why do we tell people to stop crying when the Savior we worship cried?
Why do we confuse spiritual maturity with emotional numbness?
The presence of grief does not automatically mean the absence of gratitude.
And the presence of gratitude does not require the absence of grief.
Sometimes both exist in the same trembling heart.
Sometimes thanksgiving sounds like a joyful song in a crowded church.
And sometimes it sounds like a whisper from a hospital bed.
“Jesus, I am afraid. But thank You that You have not left me.”
Sometimes it sounds like a mother praying through tears.
“Lord, I do not understand what happened to my child. But I know You hear me.”
Sometimes it sounds like a husband sitting in his car after another rejection.
“Father, I don't know how I will provide for my family. But thank You that I can still come to You.”
Sometimes it sounds like a believer who has fallen into sin again, finally abandoning excuses.
“Jesus, I have failed You. I have no righteousness of my own to offer. Thank You that Your mercy calls sinners to repentance.”
That is not shallow optimism.
That is faith reaching toward Christ while surrounded by circumstances it cannot control.
And if you have ever prayed like that, even with a shaking voice, you know how costly those words can be.
But we must go deeper.
Because the apostle Paul was not writing these words from a life untouched by suffering.
This was a man who knew persecution.
Who knew physical suffering.
Who knew rejection, danger, and imprisonment.
Who described being beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, sleepless, and exposed to hardship in 2 Corinthians 11.
And the Thessalonian believers themselves had received the Gospel amid affliction, as Paul acknowledged in 1 Thessalonians 1:6.
When Paul commanded them to give thanks in all circumstances, he was not speaking to people whose greatest difficulty was an inconvenient morning.
He was writing to Christians learning to follow Jesus in a hostile world.
And the instruction did not stand alone.
Read the surrounding passage.
“Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18
Do you see the movement?
Rejoice.
Pray.
Give thanks.
These are not three commands demanding that you deny reality.
They are three expressions of a life continually oriented toward God.
Rejoicing is rooted in the Lord, not in the pleasantness of every event.
Prayer keeps the believer in communion with God.
Thanksgiving remembers His goodness and grace even when circumstances are difficult.
And none of these commands can be separated from the words that follow.
“In Christ Jesus.”
That phrase is not decoration.
It is everything.
Without Christ, gratitude can become a desperate attempt to manufacture happiness.
But in Christ, gratitude becomes a response to grace that suffering cannot erase.
You may lose your income.
You may lose a relationship.
You may lose opportunities you prayed for.
You may even lose your physical life.
But if you belong to Jesus, the forgiveness He purchased through His blood cannot be canceled by an unexpected tragedy.
The resurrection cannot be undone by a medical report.
The promise of eternal life cannot be overturned by another person's betrayal.
And God's steadfast love cannot be measured by the balance in your bank account.
Romans 8:38–39 teaches that neither death nor life, nor anything else in creation, can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Not because suffering is imaginary.
But because Christ's love is real.
And this is where the Gospel confronts something deeper than our circumstances.
Our hearts.
Because suffering is not the only reason we struggle to give thanks.
Sometimes we struggle because we have quietly begun to believe that God owes us a life without disappointment.
We pray.
We serve.
We attend church.
We help others.
We try to obey.
And somewhere along the way, without ever saying it aloud, we begin treating obedience like a contract.
Lord, I did my part. Why didn't You do Yours?
We expected faithfulness to protect us from heartbreak.
We expected generosity to guarantee prosperity.
We expected prayer to produce the answer we wanted.
And when life refused to follow our expectations, resentment began growing in places we did not want anyone to see.
That is a painful thing to admit.
But it may also be the beginning of repentance.
Because Jesus never promised His disciples a trouble-free world.
He said in John 16:33:
“In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
Notice what He did not say.
He did not promise that believers would never suffer.
He promised that suffering would never make Him less victorious.
And Christian thanksgiving grows from that victory.
Not from the illusion that everything will happen the way we planned.
There is another Scripture we must handle carefully.
Ephesians 5:20 speaks of “giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
In Greek, the expression includes ὑπὲρ πάντων (hyper pantōn), commonly translated “for everything” or “for all things.”
So we should not claim that the Bible never calls Christians to thank God for all things.
It does use that language.
But we must read both passages together, within the whole witness of Scripture.
Ephesians does not teach that evil becomes morally good or that God delights in wickedness.
Scripture consistently condemns injustice, cruelty, oppression, and sin.
God does not command His people to approve of evil.
Rather, believers can give thanks to God amid all that He sovereignly permits, trusting His wisdom, His righteous purposes, and His ability to redeem what human beings intended for harm.
We can thank Him for His sustaining grace.
For His presence.
For the good He brings even out of circumstances that are genuinely evil.
For the final restoration He has promised in Christ.
And when we cannot identify any present good in a tragedy, we are not required to invent one.
This distinction is essential.
Because a person who has been abused does not need someone telling them to thank God for the abuse.
They need to know that God condemns evil, that their suffering matters, and that seeking safety, justice, and wise help is not a failure of faith.
A grieving parent does not need someone explaining that the death of a child is secretly wonderful.
They need the compassion of Christ, the hope of resurrection, and a community willing to mourn with those who mourn.
A struggling believer does not need a manufactured explanation for every wound.
Sometimes the most faithful response is simply to sit beside someone and weep.
And perhaps the most powerful biblical picture of this truth is found not in a comfortable room, but in the darkest injustice in human history.
The crucifixion of Jesus Christ.
Think about that Friday.
The innocent Son of God was betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Condemned.
Nailed to a Roman cross.
And as He hung there, suffering beneath the weight of human cruelty, His followers could scarcely comprehend what was happening.
From their perspective, hope itself appeared to be dying.
But Scripture reveals something astonishing.
God was accomplishing redemption through the very event that exposed humanity's sin.
In Acts 2:23, Peter teaches that Jesus was delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, while those who crucified Him remained responsible for their lawless actions.
God's sovereign purpose did not make their wickedness righteous.
Their evil was still evil.
Their injustice was still injustice.
Their sin was still sin.
But their sin could not defeat God's saving purpose.
And on the third day, the stone was rolled away.
Jesus rose.
Death was conquered.
The crucified Savior was revealed as the risen Lord.
The cross did not become good because betrayal was good. The cross is our salvation because Jesus, in His perfect love and obedience, accomplished redemption through what sinful humanity did to Him.
That is the difference.
And that is the Gospel.
God does not need evil to become good before He can demonstrate His power over it.
He is able to overcome evil without ever calling evil righteous.
Consider Joseph.
Betrayed by his brothers.
Sold into slavery.
Falsely accused.
Imprisoned.
Forgotten.
Years later, he stood before the very people who had helped destroy his childhood.
And in Genesis 50:20, he said:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
The Hebrew is especially revealing.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Attem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah.
A close rendering is:
“You planned evil against me; God planned it for good.”
The Hebrew verb חָשַׁב (chashav), appearing in different grammatical forms in this verse, carries the idea of planning, intending, or devising.
The same underlying verb is used for the brothers' evil intention and God's good purpose.
Joseph did not deny what his brothers had done.
He called it evil.
But he also recognized that their evil intentions had not overthrown God's providence.
And there is a beautiful, necessary caution here.
Joseph was eventually able to see a remarkable way God had worked through his suffering to preserve lives.
Not every suffering believer receives that kind of explanation in this life.
Some prayers remain unanswered in the way we hoped.
Some relationships are never restored.
Some losses leave empty chairs for decades.
Some questions will not be answered until we stand before the Lord.
So the promise is not that every tragedy will become understandable before you die.
The promise is that the God who raised Jesus from the dead will not abandon His redemptive purpose.
Romans 8:28 assures believers that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And the following verse identifies the deeper purpose: conformity to the image of His Son.
God's promised good is ultimately greater than earthly comfort.
It is our transformation in Christ and our final glory with Him.
That is why thanksgiving is possible even when explanations are absent.
Not because we know everything.
But because we know the One in whom our hope rests.
And now I want you to think about something personal.
Something you may have spent years avoiding.
What happened to you that made thanksgiving difficult?
Was it the person who abandoned you when you needed them most?
The betrayal that changed the way you trust?
The prayer you prayed for years that still seems unanswered?
The ministry where you were hurt by people who spoke about Jesus but failed to reflect His love?
The season when you were so overwhelmed that even opening your Bible felt exhausting?
Or was it something you did?
A hidden sin.
A decision you regret.
A relationship you damaged.
A season of rebellion you cannot undo.
Maybe you are carrying both wounds and guilt.
You have been hurt.
And you have hurt others.
You need comfort.
And you need repentance.
You need healing.
And you need forgiveness.
And the beautiful truth of the Gospel is that Jesus is sufficient for both.
He is not merely a sympathetic observer of your suffering.
He is the Savior who died for your sins and rose again.
He calls the wounded to come to Him.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
He does not minimize our wrongdoing.
He does not excuse what destroys us.
He offers forgiveness purchased through His own sacrifice and a new life shaped by His grace.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not because our tears earn forgiveness.
Not because our gratitude purchases mercy.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior who has made forgiveness possible.
And this is where thanksgiving becomes something far more beautiful than a religious obligation.
It becomes the response of a rescued sinner.
“Jesus, thank You that my worst decision does not have to define my eternal destiny.”
“Thank You that I can repent instead of hiding.”
“Thank You that Your grace does not give me permission to remain in sin, but power and reason to turn away from it.”
“Thank You that I do not have to pretend I am righteous when I can confess my need for Your righteousness.”
“Thank You that You loved me enough to die for sinners like me.”
And maybe tonight, for the first time in a long time, you can stop trying to perform gratitude.
You can simply be honest before God.
You can tell Him the truth.
“Father, I am angry.”
“Lord, I am confused.”
“Jesus, I miss them.”
“God, I am afraid of what happens next.”
“I want to trust You, but I am struggling.”
There is room in biblical prayer for such honesty.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Psalm 13 begins with David asking how long the Lord will seem to forget him.
Psalm 22 begins with the agonizing cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
And Jesus Himself quoted those opening words from the cross.
Lament is not the opposite of faith.
Biblical lament brings anguish into the presence of God rather than using anguish as a reason to flee from Him.
And sometimes that is where gratitude begins.
Not with a cheerful declaration.
But with a decision to keep praying.
Not with an explanation.
But with surrender.
Not with pretending everything is fine.
But with admitting that everything is not fine, and still turning toward Christ.
There is something else I want you to remember.
Gratitude is not a payment that purchases God's love.
You do not earn His attention by thanking Him enough.
You do not secure His forgiveness through religious performance.
You do not become worthy of salvation by learning to smile through suffering.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
And the next verse reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
Thanksgiving is fruit, not the price of admission.
That truth matters because some of you have been carrying a secret fear.
You think God is disappointed because you are not handling your suffering well enough.
You compare your tears with someone else's testimony.
You hear another Christian say they praised God immediately after tragedy, and you wonder why you cannot do the same.
You see smiling pictures of people celebrating breakthroughs while you are still waiting for yours.
And you quietly conclude that perhaps your faith is defective.
But spiritual maturity is not measured by how convincingly you conceal your wounds.
The Lord knows your heart.
He knows the difference between rebellion and exhaustion.
He knows when you are resisting His truth.
And He knows when you are desperately reaching for Him through tears.
Remember the father in Mark 9:24 who cried out:
“I believe; help my unbelief!”
What an extraordinary prayer.
Faith and struggle in the same sentence.
Belief and need in the same breath.
And he brought both to Jesus.
Perhaps your prayer tonight is not, “Lord, thank You for everything that happened.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, I still believe You are good. Help me trust You with what I cannot understand.”
That is a prayer worth praying.
Again tomorrow, if necessary.
And the next day.
Because the Christian life is not one dramatic moment of surrender followed by a lifetime without struggle.
It is a daily walk of repentance, dependence, obedience, and grace.
There will be mornings when thanksgiving comes easily.
And there will be nights when all you can say is, “Jesus, please help me.”
Keep coming to Him.
Keep opening His Word.
Keep praying.
Keep gathering with faithful believers.
Keep receiving wise help when you need it.
Keep confessing your sins rather than defending them.
Keep remembering the cross.
Because the cross tells you that God's love is not a sentimental promise spoken from a safe distance.
It is a love demonstrated through sacrifice.
And the empty tomb tells you that suffering and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
That does not erase today's pain.
But it changes the horizon beyond it.
One day, according to Revelation 21:4, God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of His people.
Death will be no more.
Neither will mourning, crying, nor pain.
Do not rush past that promise.
Every tear.
Every grief that made you feel alone.
Every night when you could not explain why you were crying.
Every sorrow that followed you into worship.
God's final restoration will not be a fragile attempt to make suffering more tolerable.
It will be the end of death and the former order of things.
And until that day, we wait with hope.
We pray.
We lament.
We repent.
We endure.
And by God's grace, we give thanks.
Not because every circumstance is good.
But because the God who has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ remains worthy of our trust.
Perhaps that is the truth someone in your life desperately needs today.
Someone who has stopped attending church because they felt judged for grieving.
Someone who believes their suffering means God has rejected them.
Someone who is smiling publicly while privately wondering whether they can keep going.
Someone who needs to hear that the Christian faith does not require them to call evil good.
Someone who needs the Gospel rather than another empty motivational slogan.
Please do not keep this message to yourself if it could help them.
Or send it privately with a simple message:
“I thought of you while reading this. You don't have to pretend you're okay. I'm praying for you.”
Because there may come a night when you need to remember that Jesus never required you to deny your grief in order to trust Him.
And if these words have reached a place in your heart that you usually keep hidden, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than a passing reaction.
It does not have to be a dramatic testimony.
Maybe your answer is simply, “His mercy.”
Maybe it is, “He has not abandoned me.”
Maybe it is, “I am still learning to trust Him.”
Not as a performance.
Not because public words make your faith more genuine.
But because your honest testimony may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
There is no shame in needing the body of Christ.
We were never meant to carry every burden alone.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious words for a few seconds.
Not to replace the local church, faithful pastors, or the fellowship every believer needs.
But to keep pointing hearts back to Scripture, repentance, the cross, the resurrection, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We want the person who is drifting from God to encounter truth.
The exhausted believer to find biblical encouragement.
The wounded Christian to be reminded of the Savior's compassion.
The unrepentant sinner to hear the loving but urgent call to turn to Christ.
And the growing disciple to find nourishment that reaches beyond a single inspirational post.
We want people to have access to resources that help them study the Bible, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, grow in prayer, pursue holiness, and follow Jesus more faithfully.
And if you believe this mission is worth strengthening, I want to invite you to become part of the people who help sustain it.

It is voluntary financial support that can help us continue producing Scripture-centered messages, developing discipleship resources, maintaining outreach, and expanding the work to reach more people with the Gospel.
But we also want to be biblically clear.
And it is certainly not a payment for God's blessing.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You do not have to pay Gospel Warrior to glorify God.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, worship, generosity, and a life increasingly shaped by His grace.
Not an obligation imposed through guilt.
A partnership offered in faith and love.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and express our gratitude to those helping sustain the mission.
You are not less valued.
You are not less faithful.
And the Gospel is not less available to you.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Sharing an article with someone who needs the truth matters.

Following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, curious seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to encounter daily Scripture and Gospel-centered teaching can help extend the reach of this work.
A single share may place a message of biblical hope before someone we could never reach personally.
A thoughtful comment may encourage someone afraid to speak.
A saved article may become a reminder of God's Word during a difficult night.
Every contribution has its place.
But none of it replaces the One who matters most.
Jesus Christ.
He is the message.
He is the Savior.
He is the reason we speak of grace.
He is the One who calls sinners to repentance, forgives those who come to Him in faith, and transforms lives by His Spirit.
And before you leave, I want you to return to the question we began with.
How am I supposed to thank God for this?
Maybe you still cannot answer it.
Maybe the wound is too fresh.
Maybe the situation has not changed.
Maybe tomorrow will still bring difficult conversations, unpaid bills, unanswered questions, or an empty chair at the dinner table.
I cannot promise that your circumstances will suddenly improve because you finished reading this article.
Scripture does not give me permission to make that promise.
But I can point you to a Savior whose death and resurrection are the foundation of a hope that does not depend on tomorrow being easy.
You can come to Him with the truth.
With your sorrow.
With your sin.
With your fear.
With your gratitude, however small it feels.
You can ask Him to forgive you.
You can ask Him to teach you to trust Him.
You can thank Him for grace while still asking Him for deliverance.
And perhaps your prayer tonight will be something like this.

“Father, I confess that there are things I do not understand. There are wounds I still carry, fears I have not overcome, and sins from which I need to turn. Forgive me for the ways I have doubted Your goodness and resisted Your Word. Thank You for sending Jesus Christ to save sinners. Thank You for His cross, His resurrection, and the promise of eternal life through Him. Teach me to give thanks in every circumstance without pretending that evil is good or that my suffering does not matter. Give me courage to grieve honestly, repent sincerely, obey faithfully, and trust You when I cannot see what You are doing. Let my life glorify Christ, not only when I am rejoicing, but also when I am learning to endure. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And now, one final thought.
The command was never meant to make you grateful for every wound.
It was meant to teach you that even in a wounded world, you have a reason to remain thankful to the God who gave His Son for you.
There is no need to pretend that what happened was good.
There is every reason to remember that Jesus is good.
The scandal of our sin met the astonishing grace of God at the cross.
The tomb that seemed to announce defeat became the place where resurrection victory was revealed.
And the sinner who once stood condemned can now be reconciled to God through faith in the risen Christ.
That is the story worth telling.
That is the grace worth sharing.
That is the Savior worth following.
You may never thank God for the moment your heart shattered, but through Jesus Christ, you can thank Him that your shattered heart is not beyond His redeeming grace.
